episodes.205852: On the 18th and 19th, abundant rainfall fell in much of our forecast area due to the remnants of a tropical storm (Mario) that moved over the eastern Pacific Ocean from along the coast of Baja California. The heaviest precipitation was reported in the Kern County desert towards the Indian Wells Valley where around 2-3 inches of rain fell on the 18th. Other locations in the San Joaquin Valley, such as Hanford and Kingsburg, exceeded one inch during the 18th into the 19th. Fresno received 0.81 inch during this period. Record high daily precipitation values were reported at Hanford on both days. Afternoon high temperatures cooled markedly during this period. On the afternoon of the 18th, a funnel cloud was also reported in the Kern County desert near Rosamond.
episodes.205901: An isolated thunderstorm initially developed over northwestern Hale County and drifted to the southeast over Hale Center (Hale County). As this storm passed over Hale Center, it produced very heavy rainfall. Although no known gauges existed in Hale Center at the time, an estimated three inches of rain fell within 30 minutes. Local broadcast media relayed a video of numerous vehicles stranded in flood waters on Interstate-27 at the Cleveland Street underpass in Hale Center.
episodes.206244: An upper level approaching shortwave ushered a cold front at the surface with an outflow boundary into Arkansas which led to multiple severe thunderstorms with large hail and damaging winds.
episodes.206400: In the early afternoon of the 19th, a cold front moving over northwestern Kansas caused  a few isolated storms to form that generally moved south-southeast, except one supercell that moved almost due east over Oberlin then moved south.  This single storm was the source for the storm reports. Hail up to 2.25 inches were reported, the largest falling in eastern Sheridan County.  The strongest reported gust was 69 MPH near Quinter.
episodes.206495: Isolated thunderstorms developed over portions of Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of September 19, 2025. While these thunderstorms were non-severe, one rogue thunderstorm in Lawrence County produced strong winds that downed a tree.
episodes.206520: During the afternoon on September 19th, a few strong to severe storms developed across Adams and Juneau Counties and produced hail of dime to quarter size before weakening into the evening hours.
episodes.206521: A monsoon storm was strong enough to produce severe size hail in Yavapai County.
episodes.206645: Widely scattered thunderstorms developed along an advancing cold front across portions of central Oklahoma during the predawn hours of the 19th. A few of these thunderstorms produced reports of thunderstorm wind damage, particularly across the northwestern corner of the Oklahoma City Metropolitan Area.
episodes.206653: Afternoon and early evening sea breeze storms produced locally heavy rainfall and gusty winds where boundaries merged across a moist and unstable airmass.
episodes.206654: Afternoon and early evening sea breeze storms produced locally heavy rainfall and gusty winds where boundaries merged across a moist and unstable airmass.
episodes.206942: During the afternoon hours of Sept 18th, storms brought damaging wind gusts to portions of western Missouri.
episodes.206963: A warm front and upper level disturbance brought scattered thunderstorms to south central WI especially north of Madison. Large hail was reported in Marquette County.
episodes.207004: The tail end of an upper trough extended southeast into the lower Ohio Valley, but the flow over west Kentucky was weak, leading to weak shear. Instability was modest with surface-based CAPE around 1000 J/kg, but that was sufficient to allow one strong storm to produce hail south of Madisonville.
episodes.207248: The combination of an upper-level low off the CA coast and the remnants of Tropical Cyclone Mario resulted in a significant moisture increase with PWATs rising to 1.5 on the 17th and upwards of 1.8-2.0 on the 18th. Thunderstorms on the 17th were concentrated mainly across the higher terrain areas of southeast CA, mainly across the Chocolate Mountains, while on the 18th, the activity was more widespread as upper-level forcing from the combination of the upper-level low and the remnants of Tropical Cyclone Mario was maximized. With MLCAPE values maxing out at 1500 J/kg along with the abundant moisture, the thunderstorms were efficient rain producers, resulting in instances of flash flooding. DCAPE values ranging between 1000-1200 J/kg also supported instances of severe damaging wind gusts.
episodes.207252: The combination of an upper-level low off the CA coast and the remnants of Tropical Cyclone Mario resulted in a significant moisture increase with PWATs increasing upwards of 1.8-2.0 across most of southwest AZ. The aforementioned features also provided strong upper-level forcing to result in widespread showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon hours.  With MLCAPE values maxing out at 1500 J/kg along with the abundant moisture, the thunderstorms were efficient rain producers, resulting in instances of flash flooding. DCAPE values ranging between 1000-1200 J/kg also resulted in instances of severe wind gusts. Further east, across Gila County, additional thunderstorm activity developed during the afternoon hours with cell training resulting in instances of flash flooding as well.
episodes.207293: Upper-level troughing off the west coast promoted a pocket of upper-level divergence over south-central AZ. With MLCAPE values ranging between 250-500 J/kg and PWAT values near 1.5, scattered thunderstorm activity with heavy rainfall rates developed across portions of the Phoenix metro area and were steered northeastward into northern Maricopa County. Although the thunderstorm activity was rather unimpactful, with the flood threat limited due to the fast steering flow, training thunderstorm activity was observed across portions of northern Maricopa County. In particular, an area near Cave Creek experienced flooding impacts during the early morning hours on the 19th with some spots observing upwards of 1.0-1.5 inches. This was enough to cause some of the washes to react, with Sonoran Wash rising above alarm stage.
episodes.207449: An upper-level wave moved across the Great plains and supported the development of supercells. There was only a small window for severe weather from each supercell moved south before weakening. After all the cells had weakened below severe and developed a small cold pool, they congealed and followed a more linear structure that tracked east.
episodes.207532: A lead shortwave on the southern periphery of a larger trough over the Central Plains was able to provide enough forcing for storms to form across east-central Arkansas during the early morning hours of September 19, 2025. An isolated storm became severe with large hail over St. Francis County.
episodes.207533: A lead shortwave on the southern periphery of a larger trough over the Central Plains was able to provide enough forcing for storms to form across east-central Arkansas during the early morning hours of September 19, 2025. These storms moved across northwest Mississippi during the morning, producing outflow boundaries that eventually resulted in new storm development over northeast Mississippi. These storms produced some damaging winds near Tupelo by early afternoon.
episodes.207586: An approaching 50+ knot jet and a mid level disturbance contributed to strong to severe thunderstorms developing along the Rio Grande Valley.  Flash flooding was reported near Radium Springs and severe wind gusts near Percha Creek.
episodes.207595: A deep tropical moisture surge contributed to the generation of showers and thunderstorms. As rain accumulated, soil became saturated, and flooding and landslides were registered. Also, wind and lightning damage was also observed within the thunderstorms.
episodes.207774: Thunderstorms moved through the Tucson Metro area on the evening of September 18th and produced locally heavy rainfall that caused washes to flow with water. Two swift water rescues occurred along the Alamo wash due to people attempting to cross in their cars. In both cases, all of the people were rescued with no injuries. The thunderstorms produced outflow winds strong enough to loft areas of blowing dust along Interstate 10 from Picacho to Eloy and reduced visibilities to less than 0.25 miles.
episodes.207851: A small but potent slow-moving thunderstorm dropped rainfall rates of 2 inches per hour for about 2 hours in a small area between Olmito and Rancho Viejo, about 11 miles north-northwest of downtown Brownsville. Minor flooding of 1 to 2 feet, mainly on poor drainage roads, was observed in the area.
episodes.207870: Moisture from the remnants of Pacific Tropical Storm Mario fueled scattered thunderstorms, many of which produced flash flooding.

Images and videos showed significant floodwaters in Pinal Creek, making low-water crossings impassable. The floodwater reached the base of a bridge located just south of Downtown Globe. Radar estimates showed over 2 inches of rain fell over the basin in less than 3 hours. No damages or injuries reported.

An SUV travelling eastbound on I-8 veered off the road, possibly due to hydroplaning, and landed upside down in a flowing wash. The two occupants were able to escape the vehicle unharmed. Timing estimated from radar.
A 63 mph peak wind gust measured at the Imperial County Airport.

Cole Blvd closed due to flooding in Calexico. Time estimated from radar. No damages or injuries reported.
Powerlines fell down and struck vehicles near the intersection of Dogwood Rd and E Aten Rd in Imperial. Wind gusts were estimated at 60-65 mph. No injuries were reported.
Semi-truck flipped over at the intersection of E Evan Hewes HWY and Bowker Rd east of El Centro. Wind gusts were estimated at 60-65 mph. No injuries reported.
CA-177 closed in both directions between I-10 and CA-62 due to flooding, with at least one car stuck in the floodwaters. No injuries reported.
There was minor flooding of Highway 395 north of Kramer Junction.
Tehachapi Willow Spring Road with Backus Road closed due to flooding.
Imler Road near Forrester Road southwest of Brawley closed due to flooding. Time estimated from radar. No damages or injuries reported.
Yocum Rd between Butters Rd and the canal east of Calipatria closed due to flooding. Time estimated from radar. No damages or injuries reported.
Cuff Rd closed between Beal Rd and Coachella Canal Rd due to flooding. Time estimated from radar. No damages or injuries reported.
Swift water rescue at E Vernice St and Birch Ave along the Alamo Wash. Occupant rescued with no injury. A nearby rain gauge recorded 0.55 inches of water in 2 hours.
Swift water rescue at East Calle Bettelgeux Rd and South Avenida Planeta Rd along the Alamo Wash. Occupant rescued without injury. A nearby rain gauge recorded 0.55 inches of water in 2 hours.
Two feet of water inundating vehicles reported along Highway 111 south of Interstate 8. No injuries reported.

Video from San Carlos Apache Police Department showed a water rescue of 5 kids and their dog who were trapped out on an island in the middle of Gilson Wash near Waco Rd. The police department received the calls for help around 2040MST. The water moving through the wash was up to the waists of the kids at the time of the rescue. A gauge several miles upstream on Gilson Wash began rising just after 1900MST and reached a peak stage of 4.2 ft at 2036MST. The floodwaters originated from a storm that produced around 2 inches of rain near Cutter. No injuries were reported.
Large amounts of half inch to three quarter inch hail fell on Utah Trail south of Highway 62.
Adobe Road was flooded between Amboy Road and Indian Trail.
The intersection of Sunfair Road and Cobalt Road was flooded.
Whistler Road driver rd to Famoso Potterville Hwy impassable and closed due to flooding.
Tree damage occurred near the intersection of Northwest 178th Street and County Line Road. The event time is estimated from radar observations.

Relayed images show damage to trees, power poles and the road sign of a church near the intersection of Northwest 234th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue. The event time is estimated from radar observations.

There were two feet of standing water at the intersection of Highways 190 and 127, water and debris over Highway 190 at Furnace Creek, and the following roads were closed: Badwater Road from Jubilee Road to Highway 190, all of West Side Road, and all of Twenty Mule Team Road.
A tree was blown down onto Arkansas Highway 14/Heber springs Road near the town of Desha.
Numerous power poles were snapped on the southern side of the town of Batesville.

A Maricopa County Flood Control District streamflow gauge on Sonoran Wash recorded floodwaters above the pre-determined alarm stage level of 2.0 feet, with the stage peaking at 2.95 feet.  The unbridged crossing at North Valley Parkway, approximately 1 mile upstream from the gauge location became impassable. A vehicle was reportedly stuck in the floodwaters requiring the driver to be rescued. Timing estimated based on the period when water levels exceeded and then receded below the alarm stage level as well as travel time for the water to reach North Valley Parkway. No  injuries reported.

Multiple trees were knocked down across Tupelo.
Tree down was knocked down across the road near CR 10.
Flooding was reported along a marginal street near PR-2, in front of a lumberyard store.
Strong thunderstorm winds downed a tree which blocked Eagle Nation Drive and Church Street near Summertown Elementary School in Summertown. Damages are a rough estimate.
Trees were knocked down along U.S. Highway 43 at the Frosty Inn.
Public reported, via social media, hail up to the size of quarters.

A small but potent slow-moving thunderstorm dropped rainfall rates of 2 inches per hour for about 2 hours in a small area between Olmito and Rancho Viejo, about 11 miles north-northwest of downtown Brownsville. Minor flooding of 1 to 2 feet, mainly on poor drainage roads, was observed in the area by a retired NWS employee.
Most of the hail was nickel to half dollar size, only a few were golf ball. Lasted around 10 minutes.
